question.en: Why should you prefer semantic HTML over styled div elements?

answer.en: Semantic elements communicate purpose, not just appearance. A `button` supplies keyboard activation and a native role; `nav`, `main`, `article`, and headings provide structure that browsers and assistive technology can expose. That usually means less JavaScript and ARIA to recreate behavior. Semantic structure also gives search engines and other tools clearer content signals. CSS can change the visual presentation without changing the meaning. I would start with the correct HTML element, keep the source order logical, and only build a custom control when native HTML cannot express the interaction.

codeBlocks.caption: Use elements whose native meaning matches the content or action.

question.en: How would you structure a page so users can navigate its regions and headings?

answer.en: I would give the document one clear primary `main` region, use `nav` for navigation, `header` and `footer` where their scope is meaningful, and use headings to describe the content hierarchy. I would make heading levels reflect the outline rather than choose them for font size. Landmark labels should distinguish repeated regions when there is more than one of the same type. The source order should make sense without CSS, because screen-reader reading order and keyboard traversal follow the document structure rather than the visual arrangement.

question.en: What makes a form control accessible, and why is a placeholder not a label?

answer.en: Each control needs a durable accessible name, normally from a visible `label` associated with its `id` and the label's `for`. The label tells users what information belongs in the control and increases the clickable target. A placeholder is only a hint: it disappears when typing and should not carry the control's identifying purpose. For related radio buttons or checkboxes, I would group them with `fieldset` and `legend`. I would also use the appropriate input type and native constraints, then provide clear instructions and errors.

codeBlocks.code:
<label for="email">Email address</label>
<input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" required />
codeBlocks.caption: An explicit label association gives the control a stable name.

sources.label: MDN: Forms and buttons in HTML

question.en: How should client-side and server-side form validation work together?

answer.en: Client-side constraints such as `required`, an input `type`, and other validation attributes give fast feedback and prevent common formatting mistakes before submission. They are a usability feature, not a security boundary: a client can disable JavaScript or send a request directly. The server must validate and safely process every submitted value. Errors should be specific, visible, associated with the affected control, and not communicated by color alone. After a failed submission, preserve entered values where appropriate and make the error summary or first invalid field reachable without creating an unexpected focus jump.

sources.label: MDN: Forms and buttons in HTML

question.en: When would you choose Flexbox over Grid, or Grid over Flexbox?

answer.en: Flexbox is primarily a one-dimensional layout tool: it distributes and aligns items along a row or column. It is a good fit for navigation links, button groups, and content inside a component. Grid models rows and columns together, so it is usually clearer for page regions or card layouts where both axes matter. They are not competing technologies; a page can use Grid for its major regions and Flexbox inside each region. I choose the simplest model that expresses the relationship, then test long content and narrow widths rather than relying on a screenshot.

codeBlocks.code:
.page { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 16rem 1fr; gap: 1rem; }
.actions { display: flex; gap: 0.5rem; align-items: center; }
codeBlocks.caption: Grid handles page tracks; Flexbox handles one-axis control alignment.

question.en: What accessibility risk comes from visually reordering Flexbox or Grid items?

answer.en: CSS visual reordering does not change the underlying DOM order. Screen readers and sequential keyboard navigation can therefore encounter links or controls in source order while sighted users see a different order. That mismatch can make a task confusing or cause focus to appear to jump around the page. I treat `order` and grid placement as visual tools only. If the order is logically wrong, I fix the HTML source order and use CSS to create the desired presentation. I test by reading the page and tabbing through every interactive element at each responsive layout.

question.en: What does mobile-first responsive design mean in practice?

answer.en: Mobile-first means starting with a usable narrow layout and adding changes when the content needs more room, rather than targeting named devices. I use flexible tracks, relative units, sensible minimum and maximum sizes, and media queries at content-driven breakpoints. The layout should remain usable between breakpoints, with no horizontal scrolling caused by fixed widths. I also include the viewport meta element so mobile browsers use the device width. Responsive testing includes zoom, keyboard navigation, long labels, and touch-sized targets—not only a few device screenshots.

codeBlocks.caption: The viewport declaration lets the layout use the device viewport width.

question.en: How does CSS decide which conflicting declaration wins?

answer.en: The cascade first considers origin and importance, then the relevant cascade layer. Specificity is compared among competing declarations in the same applicable origin and layer: IDs outweigh classes, attributes, and pseudo-classes, which outweigh type selectors and pseudo-elements. `:where()` contributes zero specificity, while `:is()`, `:not()`, and `:has()` take specificity from their most specific argument. If specificity ties, scoping proximity and then source order decide. I keep selectors low-weight and use layers or component boundaries instead of escalating specificity or reaching for `!important`.

codeBlocks.code:
:where(.card) a { color: navy; }
.card a { color: teal; }
codeBlocks.caption: The second selector has greater specificity because :where() contributes zero.

question.en: Which modern CSS features improve maintainability, and what guardrails would you use?

answer.en: I use custom properties for shared design values, cascade layers to define broad precedence deliberately, and low-specificity selectors so component styles remain overridable. `:where()` is useful when authoring defaults that should not create a specificity fight; `:has()` can express a relationship when the supported browser target permits it. CSS nesting can reduce repetition, but I still inspect the generated selector specificity. The guardrails are progressive enhancement where necessary, a documented browser-support policy, and tests for focus, zoom, contrast, overflow, and reduced-motion preferences. A newer feature is not automatically a better abstraction.

codeBlocks.caption: Tokens, layers, and zero-specificity defaults make overrides predictable.

question.en: What is WCAG, and how should a frontend engineer use it?

answer.en: WCAG is the W3C Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. It organizes requirements under four principles: content should be perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Success criteria have conformance levels, but a team should not treat a level label as a substitute for user-centered testing. I use the criteria to turn accessibility requirements into design, markup, CSS, and interaction checks—for example, keyboard operation, visible focus, text alternatives, labels, and programmatically exposed names and states. Automated checks are useful for repeatable rules, while manual keyboard and assistive-technology testing are still necessary.

question.en: When should you use ARIA, and when should you use native HTML instead?

answer.en: Native HTML is the default because the browser already supplies semantics, keyboard behavior, and accessibility-API mappings for standard controls. I add ARIA when the required role, state, property, or relationship cannot be expressed with native HTML, and then I implement the complete interaction as well. ARIA does not add behavior by itself. For example, putting a button role on a div does not automatically provide keyboard activation. I also avoid conflicting or redundant roles and verify the resulting accessible name, role, state, value, and focus behavior with inspection and manual testing.

question.en: What are name, role, state, and value, and why do they matter?

answer.en: The accessible name identifies a component to the user; the role describes what it is; states and properties expose characteristics such as expanded, checked, or disabled; and the value communicates the current user-settable value where applicable. These must be programmatically determinable and changes must be exposed to user agents and assistive technology. Standard HTML controls usually provide this contract when used correctly. For custom widgets, I explicitly design the semantic mapping, keyboard interaction, focus model, and state updates together. An ARIA attribute without matching behavior can expose a misleading interface.

codeBlocks.caption: The state and relationship must reflect the actual control behavior.

question.en: How do you make a custom interactive element keyboard accessible?

answer.en: First I ask whether a native button, link, input, or disclosure control already fits; that is safer. If custom markup is unavoidable, it needs an interactive role, a programmatically determinable name, keyboard activation equivalent to pointer activation, a sensible place in the tab order, and a visible focus indicator. A tabindex value of zero adds an element to the normal order; a value of negative one permits programmatic focus without adding it to sequential tabbing. I avoid positive tabindex values because they create a separate order that is hard to maintain and can confuse users.

codeBlocks.code:
<button class="control" type="button">Save</button>

<style>
.control:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid currentColor; outline-offset: 3px; }
</style>
codeBlocks.caption: Prefer a native button and preserve a visible focus treatment.

question.en: How should you provide alternative text for meaningful and decorative images?

answer.en: Alternative text should convey the image's relevant meaning in its context, not blindly describe every visible detail. A meaningful image gets concise `alt` text; if nearby text already communicates the same information, the alternative should not duplicate it. A purely decorative image should use an empty `alt` so assistive technology can skip it, or be supplied as CSS decoration when appropriate. An absent `alt` is not equivalent to an intentional empty alternative. If an image needs a longer explanation, provide that as surrounding text and associate it deliberately rather than putting an essay in `alt`.

codeBlocks.caption: The first image conveys identity; the second is decorative.

question.en: When would an `aria-live` region be appropriate, and how would you avoid overwhelming users?

answer.en: A live region is appropriate when content changes dynamically and the user needs the update without moving focus, such as a concise status or validation result. I prefer native elements and purpose-specific roles where they fit, keep the announced text short, and choose politeness based on urgency: routine updates should not interrupt, while urgent messages may need stronger announcement behavior. I do not put an entire frequently changing dashboard in an assertive region. I also test with the target browser and screen reader combination, because announcement timing and support are part of the real user experience.

codeBlocks.caption: A concise, non-interruptive status is a reasonable live-region use.

question.en: What should an accessible focus indicator and hover-triggered disclosure do?

answer.en: Every keyboard-focusable control needs a visible focus indicator, and it must remain visible while focus is present. I preserve the browser indicator or replace it with a sufficiently clear, contrasting style rather than removing it. If hover or focus reveals additional content, users need a way to dismiss it without moving focus, the pointer must be able to move into the content without it disappearing, and the content should persist until the trigger is left, it is dismissed, or it is no longer valid. The pattern must work with keyboard, touch, zoom, and assistive technology—not only a mouse.

codeBlocks.caption: Keep focus visible; style can be customized without removing the indication.

question.en: Which HTML choices provide a sound SEO foundation?

answer.en: I start with meaningful, crawlable content in the HTML: a descriptive document title, the correct language declaration, a logical heading hierarchy, descriptive link text, semantic sections, and useful text alternatives for meaningful images. Navigation should use real links with URLs, not clickable spans that only work after JavaScript runs. The page should remain understandable in source order and at different viewport sizes. These practices primarily improve structure, usability, and interpretation; they are not a promise of a ranking position. SEO basics and accessibility often align because both benefit from clear, honest document semantics.

question.en: How would you design a responsive navigation that remains accessible when it collapses?

answer.en: I would keep navigation as real links inside a `nav`, provide a native button to open and close the compact menu, and expose its state with `aria-expanded` and its controlled region with `aria-controls` when needed. The closed panel should not remain in the keyboard or accessibility tree. The toggle itself needs a clear name and visible focus. On open, focus management must be predictable; on close, return focus to the toggle if the user initiated the close. I test the full flow with keyboard, touch, zoom, narrow widths, and a screen reader, including the case where JavaScript is delayed or fails.

codeBlocks.caption: The button exposes state; the links remain native navigation.

question.en: How would you choose breakpoints for a component library used in many layouts?

answer.en: I would avoid encoding a device catalog into every component. The breakpoint should represent where the component's content or interaction becomes unusable, and the base style should remain a valid narrow layout. For reusable components, container-based decisions can be more appropriate than viewport-based decisions because the same component may live in a sidebar, modal, or full-width region. I would define tokens and a support policy, use flexible Grid or Flexbox tracks before adding breakpoints, and test intermediate widths, zoom, long text, and localization. The architecture should preserve semantic source order and keep responsive changes from changing logical focus order.

question.en: How should a client-rendered route change be made understandable to keyboard and screen-reader users?

answer.en: A client-rendered route change should update the document title and provide a clear focus destination in the new view, commonly the page heading or a main-region target. Focus should not remain on a control that disappeared, and it should not be moved without a meaningful reason. The new content needs correct headings, landmarks, names, and states so assistive technology can understand it. I preserve normal link semantics and browser history, announce only what is useful, and test back/forward navigation, deep links, loading and error states, keyboard traversal, and screen-reader reading order. The implementation belongs in the routing/accessibility platform layer rather than every page.
